summary: A Mind the Interior blog article by a designer asks whether designers should lead or follow design trends. It argues trends reflect society and deserve understanding rather than dismissal, but designers should design for clients and their own style, taking bits of trends rather than following them blindly. It covers how trends arise (pop culture, Pantone's Colour of the Year) and warns against becoming a trend addict.
one_line: A blog essay arguing designers should understand design trends but design for clients and personal style rather than follow trends blindly.
key_facts: The article is titled 'LEADING VS. FOLLOWING DESIGN TRENDS – what should I do?' and was published on September 8, 2019 on Mind the Interior.
The author noticed five pairs of the same shoes as hers at a yoga class entrance, prompting reflection on fitting in through trends.
Lori Weitzner, author of Ode to Color, says trends are heavily influenced by pop culture, fashion, food, music, the streets, and sometimes world politics.
Pantone calls itself 'the global authority on colour' and has crowned a Colour of the Year since 2000.
The Pantone Color Institute is a 20-person team that begins global research early in the spring, and the process now takes nearly nine months.
Pantone describes its Colour of the Year as 'a colour snapshot of what we see taking place in our global culture that serves as an expression of a mood and an attitude.'
Pantone's color of the year 2019 was PANTONE 16-1546 Living Coral.
Kaitlyn Ellison says trends are how we interpret what has happened before to help us understand and predict the future.
Kaitlyn Ellison notes trends tend to be cyclical, so a trend is likely to come back around at some point in some form.
The author states that trends should not be pushed aside and stigmatised just because of their popularity, since they tell us something about society.
The author argues: 'If you always design for a trend you will in time be outdated and have to scramble for every trend coming out.'
The article's bottom line is that designers should design for their clients and not for themselves, leaving the designer's ego out of it.
The author says that as much as she likes clean, minimal Scandinavian interiors, it would not work for her because she loves colour, patterns and collects antiques and plants.
The article concludes that designers should take what they need from trends, disregard the rest, and balance making something unique and bold with familiar and safe.
The article quotes Iman: 'There is a lot of noise out there. I don't want to follow the trend – I want to create the trend.'
